title: World War II
subtitle: Twenty-one choices, from the prewar years to the aftermath.
introNote: An expanded selection of 18 films and three complete miniseries, including all three Spielberg–Hanks companion dramas. Choose the perspectives that interest you: several titles overlap. Watching everything is about 73 hours, using approximately an hour per series episode. IMDb scores were checked on 26 October 2026 using publicly indexed pages and can change; they are not historical-accuracy scores.
scopeNote: This expanded route adds major popular films, the bomber war, captivity and the Burma–Thailand railway to the original selection. It remains selective: the wider Eastern Front, mainland Italy, the longer war in China, Southeast Asian campaigns and colonial experiences need more attention. Labels distinguish historical depiction, context, fictional missions and alternate history.
closingNote: Germany surrendered in May 1945; Japan announced surrender in August and signed on 2 September. The chart extends into 1946 because The Pacific devotes a substantial final episode to homecoming and readjustment, not merely an old-age epilogue. Films are selected for engaging viewing, not as substitutes for the historical sources.

events.title: Dictatorship and rearmament
events.description: Hitler became chancellor in 1933 and dismantled German democracy. Rearmament challenged the post-WWI order. The Gathering Storm approaches these dangers through Churchill’s warnings and domestic difficulties in Britain; it is background to Nazi expansion, not a history of Hitler’s rise.

events.title: The war in Asia is already underway
events.description: Full-scale war between China and Japan began in 1937, years before Pearl Harbor. Japanese forces captured Nanjing that December and committed mass atrocities against civilians and prisoners. City of Life and Death places that violence at the centre of the route.

sources.label: National WWII Museum · War in China
National Museum of the Pacific War · Timeline

events.title: Munich and the limits of appeasement
events.description: Britain and France accepted Germany’s annexation of the Sudetenland at Munich, under pressure from Hitler and without Czechoslovakia at the negotiations. Read this after The Gathering Storm: its central story ends earlier and its 1939 coda does not fill in Munich.

events.title: Poland is invaded; Europe goes to war
events.description: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September; Britain and France declared war two days later. The Soviet Union invaded from the east on 17 September. Schindler’s List begins in the resulting German occupation, rather than reconstructing the invasion itself.

events.title: Supply lines are a battlefield
events.description: German U-boats attacked the merchant shipping on which Britain and the Allied war effort depended. Escorts, intelligence, aircraft and industrial production gradually changed the balance. Das Boot follows the German side of one patrol in 1941, not the entire Atlantic campaign.

sources.label: US Navy Museum · Battle of the Atlantic

events.title: France falls; an army escapes
events.description: Germany’s western offensive trapped Allied armies near Dunkirk. An evacuation saved roughly 338,000 troops, but left equipment behind and did not prevent France’s defeat. Dunkirk makes the escape immediate; its interwoven time scales all remain within 1940.

events.title: The battle moves into the air
events.description: The Luftwaffe failed to gain the air superiority needed for a German invasion of Britain. Radar, organisation, aircraft production and aircrew from several countries mattered alongside the pilots. Dunkirk supplies an earlier view of RAF combat, not a depiction of this later air campaign.

sources.label: Royal Air Force · Battle of Britain

events.title: Occupation, collaboration and resistance
events.description: Occupied Europe contained repression, collaboration, survival and many forms of resistance. In France, clandestine networks grew under German occupation and Vichy rule. Inglourious Basterds borrows this setting for an invented revenge story; its plot must not replace the real history of resistance or liberation.

sources.label: French Ministry of the Armed Forces · Resistance

events.title: Hitler attacks the Soviet Union
events.description: Operation Barbarossa opened an immense eastern war of conquest and annihilation, accompanied by mass murder. The invasion failed to secure a quick victory. Read this before Enemy at the Gates, which begins later at Stalingrad rather than depicting Barbarossa.

sources.label: USHMM · Invasion of the Soviet Union

events.title: Persecution becomes systematic genocide
events.description: Nazi Germany and its collaborators murdered six million Jews. War, occupation, mass shootings, deportations and killing centres were integral to this genocide. Schindler’s List follows persecution, forced labour and rescue around Kraków; it is one story within a much larger crime.

events.title: Pearl Harbor makes the war global
events.description: Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on 7 December as it launched wider offensives in Asia and the Pacific. The United States entered the war; Germany and Italy then declared war on it. Tora! Tora! Tora! follows Japanese planning and American failures before the attack.

sources.label: National Museum of the Pacific War · Timeline

events.title: The Pacific initiative begins to shift
events.description: US carrier aircraft sank four Japanese carriers at Midway in June 1942. The Guadalcanal campaign began in August. Midway now supplies a direct cinematic depiction of the carrier battle; The Pacific follows Marines at Guadalcanal. Pearl Harbor’s Doolittle Raid is earlier context, not Midway itself.

sources.label: National Museum of the Pacific War · Timeline

events.title: Stalingrad reverses the eastern campaign
events.description: The battle for Stalingrad consumed German and Soviet armies. Soviet encirclement trapped the German Sixth Army, which surrendered in early 1943. Enemy at the Gates uses a heavily dramatised sniper rivalry to enter this battle; it is not an account of the whole Soviet victory.

events.title: The Allies gain ground in North Africa
events.description: Victory at El Alamein and the Anglo-American Torch landings squeezed Axis forces between armies advancing from east and west. The remaining Axis forces surrendered in Tunisia in May 1943. This secured the next stage of the Mediterranean campaign. Patton joins the story in Tunisia in 1943, after El Alamein and Torch.

events.title: Captivity, forced labour and escape
events.description: Prisoner experiences varied sharply by captor, theatre and status. The Burma–Thailand railway exploited Allied POWs and a far larger Asian civilian workforce. The Great Escape dramatises a European airmen’s breakout; Masters of the Air also follows captured crews. These are distinct systems and stories, not interchangeable prison experiences.

events.title: Italy is not a shortcut
events.description: The Allies invaded Sicily and mainland Italy in 1943. Mussolini fell and Italy signed an armistice, but German occupation and difficult terrain prolonged the fighting. The campaign continued alongside the later Normandy offensive, rather than ending when D-Day began. Patton depicts the Sicilian stage.
events.gapNote: The Sicily link does not imply coverage of the later mainland fighting at Salerno, Cassino or Anzio.

events.title: The bomber war over Europe
events.description: US bomber crews flew from Britain against targets in German-held Europe, suffering heavy losses to fighters and anti-aircraft fire. Masters of the Air follows the 100th Bomb Group from 1943. This adds the US daylight-bomber perspective; it is not a complete account of Allied air strategy or the civilian experience of bombing.

sources.label: National WWII Museum · Masters of the Air and the bomber war
Apple TV · Series and episode guide

events.title: The western Allies return to France
events.description: D-Day opened the Normandy landings, followed by a hard-fought campaign inland. Saving Private Ryan begins on Omaha Beach and follows a fictional rescue mission. Band of Brothers supplies the airborne-company perspective. Neither covers the full multinational invasion on its own.

sources.label: Amblin · Band of Brothers and its campaigns

events.title: The advance stalls and counterattacks
events.description: The attempt to cross the Rhine through the Netherlands failed at Arnhem. Germany then attacked in the Ardennes, producing the Battle of the Bulge. Band of Brothers covers Market Garden and the fighting around Bastogne, showing why victory was not immediate after Normandy. Patton adds an army-command perspective on the relief of Bastogne.

sources.label: Amblin · Band of Brothers and its campaigns

events.title: The island campaigns grow more costly
events.description: Peleliu, Iwo Jima and Okinawa reveal different stages of the advance towards Japan. The Pacific follows Marines through these battles. Hacksaw Ridge adds an Army medic’s story at Okinawa. Both focus on people in ground combat rather than the whole naval and air campaign.

sources.label: National Museum of the Pacific War · Timeline

events.title: Camps are liberated; Germany collapses
events.description: Soviet and western Allied armies liberated camps as they entered German-held territory. Soviet forces took Berlin; Germany surrendered in May. Downfall portrays the regime’s collapse, while Fury invents a tank crew’s ordeal. The series and Schindler’s List add aircrew, liberation and rescue perspectives.

events.title: Bombing, Soviet entry and Japan’s surrender
events.description: Conventional bombing devastated Japanese cities. The US atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and Soviet entry into the war in August preceded Japan’s surrender announcement on 15 August and formal signing on 2 September. Grave of the Fireflies shows civilian survival after Kobe’s firebombing, not the atomic attacks.
events.gapNote: The atomic bombings and Soviet offensive are essential context, but are not directly reconstructed by these selections. The Pacific includes news of surrender and its consequences.

events.title: Home is not an instant recovery
events.description: Demobilisation brought relief alongside grief, displacement and lasting trauma. The Pacific’s final episode spends substantial time with veterans trying to resume civilian life, including Eugene Sledge’s 1946 homecoming. That is why its bar extends beyond the fighting in 1945.

entries.title: The Gathering Storm
entries.premise: Winston Churchill struggles with money, marriage and political isolation while trying to raise the alarm about German rearmament. A compact political opening before the battlefield stories.
entries.learn: Why warnings about Hitler competed with a powerful desire to avoid another war. This is a Churchill-centred perspective, not a neutral survey of British policy.
entries.coverageNote: The sustained story is concentrated in 1934–1936. Exclude the short September 1939 return-to-office coda; it does not establish continuous coverage of 1937–1939. The International Churchill Society specifically notes the narrative jump after 1936. This is the 2002 Albert Finney film, not the 1974 version.

sources.label: International Churchill Society · The film and its time jump

entries.title: City of Life and Death
entries.premise: Chinese soldiers, civilians and a Japanese soldier experience the fall and occupation of Nanjing. A stark drama that begins the Asian story before the European war.
entries.learn: The scale and brutality of the war in China, and the precarious protection offered by the Nanjing Safety Zone. The characters combine historical and fictional material.
entries.coverageNote: Late 1937 into early 1938: the fall of Nanjing and the ensuing weeks of occupation and atrocities. The two-year label reflects the calendar boundary, not two full years of action. Film synopses often abbreviate this to 1937; the massacre and occupation story extends into the following year.

sources.label: National WWII Museum · War in China

entries.title: Schindler’s List
entries.premise: Oskar Schindler arrives in occupied Poland seeking profit, then uses his factory to protect Jewish workers as Nazi persecution intensifies.
entries.learn: Occupation, ghettos, forced labour and rescue within the Holocaust. The focus on a rescuer should not obscure the victims’ lives or the vast scale of the genocide.
entries.coverageNote: The central narrative runs from the German occupation in 1939 through the end of the war in 1945. Exclude the modern-day graveside epilogue. This is a selective dramatic rescue narrative, not coverage of every year’s military campaigns or every part of the Holocaust.

sources.label: National WWII Museum · Schindler and occupied Poland chronology

entries.title: Dunkirk
entries.premise: Soldiers on a beach, civilians in a small boat and RAF pilots converge during the evacuation from France. Three different time scales make the rescue feel like a race.
entries.learn: How an evacuation preserved troops while leaving a military catastrophe behind. The suspense is strongest at the individual level, rather than in explanations of strategy.
entries.coverageNote: May–June 1940 only. The film intercuts a week on land, a day at sea and an hour in the air; these are overlapping durations within the same operation, not separate story years. Characters and incidents are largely fictionalised.

entries.title: Das Boot
entries.premise: A German submarine crew moves between suffocating boredom and sudden terror during an Atlantic patrol. Use the 149-minute theatrical film for this route.
entries.learn: The human and technical strain of submarine warfare, seen from inside a U-boat. Read the event note for the merchant crews, escorts and supply struggle outside this viewpoint.
entries.coverageNote: Autumn–winter 1941. This is Wolfgang Petersen’s 1981 film, not the later television series. The total uses the 149-minute theatrical cut; the director’s cut is about 208–209 minutes and the uncut television version is longer. Longer editions do not turn it into coverage of the whole Atlantic war.

entries.title: Tora! Tora! Tora!
entries.premise: Japanese preparations and American warning failures unfold towards the attack on Pearl Harbor. The parallel perspectives make the escalation easier to follow.
entries.learn: How planning, intelligence and command decisions converged in December 1941. Its emphasis on the attack should be read alongside Japan’s wider war in China and Southeast Asia.
entries.coverageNote: The main plot is the planning and execution of the December 1941 attack. Brief earlier setup, including Yamamoto’s 1939 appointment, does not extend the main-story bar. Runtime uses IMDb’s 144-minute listing; edition timings vary. Reconstructed dialogue is not a transcript of historical conversations.

sources.label: Film history · Opening and attack preparations
National Museum of the Pacific War · Timeline

entries.title: Pearl Harbor
entries.premise: Two pilots and a nurse are caught in a love triangle that stretches across the attack on Hawaii and the Doolittle Raid. Michael Bay puts romance and blockbuster spectacle ahead of a campaign overview.
entries.learn: A popular dramatic route into Pearl Harbor and the American response. The 6.3 IMDb score is visibly lower than most of this list; Tora! Tora! Tora! remains the stronger companion for understanding the attack’s planning.
entries.coverageNote: The main adult story covers 1941 and the April 1942 Doolittle Raid. Exclude the 1923 childhood opening and the brief later family epilogue. The central characters and romance are fictional, and the RAF material alters historical chronology. The Doolittle connection supplies context before Midway, not a depiction of that battle.

sources.label: Disney D23 · Official film identity and runtime
US Naval Institute · Attack and April 1942 raid

eventNotes.midway: Doolittle Raid: earlier context, not Midway

entries.title: Midway
entries.premise: American naval aviators and intelligence officers move from Pearl Harbor towards the carrier battle at Midway. Roland Emmerich supplies a large-scale, effects-heavy view of the Pacific air-and-sea war.
entries.learn: How carrier aviation, codebreaking and risk shaped an early Pacific turning point. Its lower IMDb score makes it a spectacle-led alternative, while it fills the original route’s missing direct depiction of Midway.
entries.coverageNote: The main war narrative runs from Pearl Harbor in December 1941 through the Doolittle Raid and Midway in 1942. Exclude the brief 1937 diplomatic setup. This is the 2019 film, not the 1976 film of the same name. Combat incidents and dialogue are compressed and dramatised.

sources.label: TIME · The film’s battle and historical setting

entries.title: The Pacific
entries.premise: Follow Robert Leckie, John Basilone and Eugene Sledge from enlistment into successive Pacific campaigns and their return home. Watch the complete ten-part miniseries.
entries.learn: How Guadalcanal, Peleliu, Iwo Jima and Okinawa felt to US Marines, and why survival did not mean an easy return to civilian life. It supplies a sustained ground-war perspective.
entries.coverageNote: The narrative begins with enlistment and family decisions after Pearl Harbor in December 1941, moves into Guadalcanal in 1942, and continues through combat in 1945. The final episode substantially follows homecoming into 1946, so that year is included. Later biographical captions and documentary framing do not extend the bar. Budget approximately ten hours.

sources.label: IMDb · Homecoming six months after V-J Day

entries.title: Enemy at the Gates
entries.premise: A Soviet sniper becomes a symbol during the fighting in Stalingrad, while a German marksman hunts him. The rivalry gives an immense battle a focused dramatic hook.
entries.learn: The destruction and pressure of urban combat on the Eastern Front. Use the historical notes to separate the real battle from the film’s romance, propaganda and sniper legend.
entries.coverageNote: The sustained sniper story takes place in 1942. Exclude the childhood prologue and the brief 1943 hospital reunion after the battle. Stalingrad itself lasted into February 1943; that event span is not the film’s main-plot span. The celebrated duel is disputed, and the film’s depiction of Soviet tactics is heavily dramatised.

sources.label: IMDb · Main story and the two-month-later coda

entries.title: Hacksaw Ridge
entries.premise: Desmond Doss enlists as a medic while refusing to carry a weapon. His struggle to remain in the army leads to the rescue of wounded soldiers on Okinawa.
entries.learn: The role of a combat medic, conscientious conviction and the human cost of the Okinawa fighting. Its faith and survival narrative complements the Marine viewpoint in The Pacific.
entries.coverageNote: The substantial enlistment, courtship and training story belongs to 1942; the combat plot jumps to Okinawa in 1945. Separate bars preserve the unshown 1943–1944 interval. Exclude the brief childhood setup and later documentary interviews. The film compresses events and omits Doss’s earlier Pacific campaigns; it is not a full service chronology.

sources.label: TIME · Enlistment, marriage, training and Okinawa

entries.title: The Great Escape
entries.premise: Allied airmen turn a German prison camp into a tunnelling operation. The ensemble, ingenuity and Steve McQueen’s escape attempt make it a classic adventure.
entries.learn: The organisation and improvisation behind escape from captivity. It borrows a real breakout but reshapes participants and action for a Hollywood ensemble.
entries.coverageNote: A year-level 1942–1944 range follows AFI’s dating of the camp arrival and the March 1944 breakout. The film explicitly compresses time and place, and catalogue summaries differ on the opening year. The famous motorcycle escape is invented, and Americans are given a larger role than in the actual breakout.

sources.label: AFI · Film chronology and compressed history

entries.title: The Bridge on the River Kwai
entries.premise: A British colonel becomes consumed by building a railway bridge for his Japanese captors while an Allied team plans to destroy it. David Lean turns captivity into a conflict over duty and pride.
entries.learn: An entry into the Burma–Thailand railway and forced-labour system, through a fictional military drama. Read the event note for the much larger Asian civilian workforce outside its main viewpoint.
entries.coverageNote: The central bridge-building and commando plot is set in 1943. The bridge’s dramatic destruction is fictional, not the real bridges’ later wartime history. Colonel Nicholson is a fictional character, not a fair portrayal of the real Philip Toosey. The 161-minute IMDb edition is used.

sources.label: TCM · Fiction and the real bridges
Australian War Memorial · Railway and forced labour

entries.title: Patton
entries.premise: George S. Patton rebuilds a shaken US force in Tunisia, competes for glory in Sicily and leads an army across western Europe. George C. Scott makes the general’s contradictions the engine of the film.
entries.learn: How North Africa and Sicily connect to the later western European campaign, and how military skill, ambition and political judgement could pull in different directions.
entries.coverageNote: The main wartime narrative runs from Tunisia in 1943 through Sicily, France, the Ardennes and Germany in 1945. Its stylised opening speech does not add another story period. This is a selective biography: Patton was not present at every campaign or battle discussed, and the film simplifies commanders’ rivalries. The 172-minute IMDb edition is used.

sources.label: US Army · Sicily and the wider campaign

entries.title: Masters of the Air
entries.premise: The men of the 100th Bomb Group fly from Britain into the air war over Europe, then face loss, captivity and the approach of victory. Watch all nine episodes of the Apple TV miniseries.
entries.learn: The US bomber campaign, the vulnerability of aircrews and the lives of captured airmen. This is the air-war companion from Spielberg, Hanks and Goetzman to Band of Brothers and The Pacific.
entries.coverageNote: The central narrative runs from deployment to England in 1943 through bombing operations, imprisonment and the end of the war in 1945. Do not add the earlier formation dates of the real unit or the later lives described in end captions. The budget uses nine episodes at approximately an hour each; actual episode lengths vary.

sources.label: Apple TV · Official series and episode guide
National WWII Museum · Masters of the Air

entries.title: Band of Brothers
entries.premise: Easy Company trains in Georgia, drops into Normandy and fights across western Europe. Watch all ten episodes, from Currahee to Points.
entries.learn: How one airborne company connects training, D-Day, Market Garden, Bastogne and the advance into Germany. Its continuity makes the later European campaign easier to remember.
entries.coverageNote: Training begins in 1942, followed by preparation and combat through 1945. Exclude the veterans’ later interviews and biographical captions. Its camp-liberation episode covers a Dachau satellite camp, not Auschwitz. Incidents and character portrayals are compressed; the series remains one US unit’s perspective. Budget approximately ten hours.

sources.label: Amblin · Band of Brothers and its campaigns

entries.title: Saving Private Ryan
entries.premise: After landing on Omaha Beach, a US squad crosses Normandy to find a paratrooper whose brothers have been killed. Spielberg and Hanks give D-Day and its aftermath an immediate human scale.
entries.learn: The shock of the landings and the confusion of fighting inland. The opening depicts a real operation; the squad, rescue mission and final village battle are fictionalised.
entries.coverageNote: June 1944 only: the beach landing and the subsequent Normandy mission are the main plot. Exclude the present-day cemetery scenes at the beginning and end. The fictional village of Ramelle and its bridge battle are not a separate documented campaign.

entries.title: Inglourious Basterds
entries.premise: A Jewish-American commando unit and a cinema owner pursue converging revenge plots in occupied France. Tarantino turns the setting into a tense, darkly comic thriller.
entries.learn: A memorable fictional encounter with occupation, antisemitic persecution and propaganda. The climax deliberately rewrites history: this is alternate history, not an explanation of how the Nazi regime actually fell.
entries.coverageNote: Two substantial narrative sections: the 1941 opening chapter establishes Shosanna’s story, while the main converging plots take place in 1944. The first chapter is part of the central causal story, rather than an old-age framing scene. Do not fill in 1942–1943 between them. Characters, operations and the film’s ending are invented.

entries.title: Downfall
entries.premise: As Soviet forces close on Berlin, Hitler’s inner circle retreats into the bunker. Traudl Junge’s viewpoint gives the collapse a claustrophobic centre.
entries.learn: The regime’s denial and disintegration during the final battle for Berlin. The bunker viewpoint explains neither the whole German population nor the much larger Soviet campaign.
entries.coverageNote: April–May 1945 is the central narrative. Exclude Junge’s brief recruitment scene in 1942, later documentary interview material and end captions. The conversations are dramatic reconstructions drawn from accounts and memoirs, not recordings of the bunker.

sources.label: Plot chronology · 1942 prologue and 1945 main story

entries.title: Fury
entries.premise: A replacement soldier joins a battered American Sherman crew during the advance into Germany. Brad Pitt’s commander holds the crew together through a series of increasingly dangerous encounters.
entries.learn: A ground-level view of armoured warfare and the brutal final phase in Germany. Its invented engagements provide tension rather than a map of the actual campaign.
entries.coverageNote: April 1945. The tank crew, isolated crossroads defence and principal combat incidents are fictional. The film’s close-range tank duels and survival story should not be treated as an account of a named historical battle or typical Sherman tactics.

entries.title: Grave of the Fireflies
entries.premise: Two siblings struggle to survive after the firebombing of Kobe. Animation makes this an intimate civilian story, with no relief from the consequences of war.
entries.learn: How bombing, hunger and the breakdown of ordinary support could destroy lives away from the front. This closes the route with civilians rather than military victory.
entries.coverageNote: The siblings’ central story takes place in 1945. The opening also belongs to 1945; exclude the brief modern-city image at the end. The bombing is conventional incendiary bombing of Kobe, not Hiroshima or Nagasaki. The story is adapted from Akiyuki Nosaka’s semi-autobiographical fiction.
